subsubtopic: MOTOR VESSEL "NORTHERN SHELL"
speechtext:
1.	With respect to the rescue of the Motor Vessel Shell, trapped in ice in Hudson Bay in September, October and November of 1972 (a) of what registry was the Shell (b) was it certified for ice operations and, if not, for what reason (c) were any non-Canadian tugs involved in the rescue and, if so, for what reason (d) what assistance and by what ships, if any, was given by the government to this ship (e) what was the cost of this assistance (f) was any damage done to Canadian ships in this operation and, if so, what was the amount of such damage (g) what was the nationality of the crew of this vessel (h) what damage was incurred by the Shell (i) what was the cargo carried by the Shell, what was its destination and what was its point of origin?
2.	What winds and other weather factors were present when decisions were taken to the effect that no emergency existed?
3.	What was the amount of user charges laid against the shipper or ship owner by Canadian authorities?
4.	What is government policy with respect to such user charges?
5.	What is the policy of other governments, such as that of the USSR, with Arctic coasts in terms of user charges?
6.	Who would have paid for damages resulting from any oil spills that such entrapment might have caused?
7.	Under what type of permit did this vessel enter Canadian waters?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MOTOR VESSEL "NORTHERN SHELL"
speechtext:
I am informed by the Departments of Transport and National Revenue as follows: 1. There is no ship by the name of Shell in our records, but we assume that the question refers to the Northern Shell; (a) British (At present the ship is registered at Hamilton, Bermuda); (b) No. At the time the vessel sustained damage there was no regulatory requirement in force calling for mandatory ice-strengthening; (c) Yes, they were engaged by Shell Oil Canadian Tankers (1964) Ltd. We are informed that Canadian tugs were not available at that time; (d) The Northern Shell was assisted by the CCGS Norman McLeod Rogers, Labrador

and the John A. Macdonald; (e) $25,000; (f) No; (g) Officers were Canadian; crew was Spanish; (h) She had suffered damage to her rudder; (i) Heating fuel and gasoline for Deception Bay from Montreal.
2.	The Northern Shell was alongside the wharf at Deception Bay and weather conditions were not so severe as to constitute an emergency or rescue situation. However, temperatures were below freezing and the ice cover was such that it was urgent to tow the vessel out to open water to prevent her being trapped in ice all winter.
3.	$25,000.
4.	The policy is to charge for services which are beyond the normal services rendered by icebreakers to ships in ice. In this instance, the services included towing a vessel which was not in any danger at the time and this task was undertaken only because the tugs present were either not capable or willing to tow a vessel of that size in the ice conditions that existed at that place and time.
5.	The current policy of other governments on user charges is not known. However, it is understood that some governments including that of the USSR charge for icebreaker assistance to commercial vessels.
6.	The owners of Northern Shell.
7.	A permit was not required at that time. The M/V Northern Shell, being a British built, British registry vessel, was entitled to engage in the coasting trade of Canada. This voyage was properly reported outwards at customs from Montreal for Deception Bay, on August 7, 1972.

speechtext: What plans, if any, exist for the development of television studio production facilities in Fredericton, New Brunswick to enable that capital city of the Province of New Brunswick to better disseminate provincial and local news and share its cultural and educational facilities with viewers in other parts of the Province and Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. James Hugh Faulkner (Secretary of State):
subsubtopic: TELEVISION STUDIO PRODUCTION FACILITIES IN FREDERICTON, N.B.
speechtext: I am informed by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as follows: The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation does not have, at present, any plans for further development of television studio production facilities in Fredericton, New Brunswick. In 1969 the CBC planned applications for an English language television system which would have involved, initially, a "mother" station to serve Saint-John-Fredericton, a rebroadcaster at Moncton, and eventual extension to the rest of New Brunswick, but the plan was turned down by the CRTC. An alternative for the CBC is to purchase one of the two privately-owned television operations in New Brunswick. There is no indication however that either of these operations is available for purchase.
